seasons.review_body: What's Wrong with Secretary Kim launched on tvN in June 2018 and peaked at 8.665 percent cable viewership (Nielsen Korea, nationwide), confirming it as one of that year's dominant romantic comedies. The show's central engine is the rapport between Park Seo-joon's gloriously self-absorbed Lee Young-joon and Park Min-young's Kim Mi-so - a dynamic that generated off-screen dating speculation at the height of the broadcast run and earned the drama a reputation as 2018's most irresistible rom-com. The series folds a childhood trauma subplot into the comic workplace premise, giving the back half genuine dramatic stakes without abandoning the tone. The IMDb audience score sits at 8.0 across a significant voter base. Its influence endures: by 2025, four separate country remakes had been produced or announced - Philippines, Thailand, China, and Indonesia - a measure of the original's export appeal.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# What's Wrong With Secretary Kim S01E01: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

**Kim Mi So** quits, and **Lee Yeong Joon** treats the news like a clerical mistake. He reaches for solutions that make sense in his world: status, money, a better title, a rearranged future with himself still at the centre. The problem is that Mi So is not negotiating. She is trying to leave a life that has turned her into a function. The episode's cleanest joke is also its sharpest argument: the Vice Chairman can command a room, manage a company image crisis, and offer a promotion on instinct, but he cannot understand a person who no longer wants to be useful to him.

## A Resignation Treated Like a System Error

The hour opens in pressure mode. During working hours, an executive director is confronted over receiving sexual services, and the language around the scene is corporate damage control. The concern is company image. Private mess becomes professional risk. People become problems to contain. Scandal becomes optics.

Into that machine comes Mi So's resignation, and the episode instantly finds its comic engine. Someone tells the Vice Chairman, "you should look for a new secretary." The line lands like a glitch report. It is practical, simple, and impossible for Yeong Joon to process.

BollyAI's read: the pilot's best idea is that Yeong Joon does not react like a lover at first. He reacts like an executive whose finest system has stopped functioning. That is funnier than panic and more revealing than sadness. The employees' reaction when Mi So says she is really quitting expands the point. Her departure is not treated as one woman's decision. It becomes an office event, a disturbance in the hierarchy.

The writing uses that disturbance to define the couple without forcing romance too early. Mi So's exit has weight because the episode keeps framing it through business procedure. She has to keep saying the obvious because everyone around her keeps hearing something else. She wants out. The workplace keeps looking for the form she forgot to fill.

## The Promotion Is the Wrong Cure

Yeong Joon's first instinct is revealing. He offers the wrong solution with full confidence: "I'll promote you to a director position!" The offer is concrete, generous in corporate terms, and useless in human terms. That is the pilot's thesis in one beat. Yeong Joon can increase her value inside the company, but Mi So is questioning the cost of being valuable only there.

The promotion is not a stupid offer. In another workplace story, it would be the reward. Here, it is the trap dressed as recognition. Mi So's problem is not that her chair is too small. The chair still belongs to the same room, the same man, the same rhythm. A director title keeps her close. It upgrades the cage.

The middle stretch shifts into business and romance banter, and the pilot finds a workable tempo there. Yeong Joon pushes with status. Mi So resists with clarity. The humour comes from mismatch rather than punchline. He thinks he has escalated the deal. She knows he has misunderstood it.

Where the episode wobbles is repetition. The resignation arc circles the same misunderstanding more than once, and the hour leans on the gap between what Yeong Joon thinks is happening and what Mi So means. The gap is funny, but it cannot carry every scene. The best moments sharpen the reason for her leaving instead of restating that he is shocked.

Still, the promotion beat gives the pilot its most efficient character writing. Yeong Joon is not painted as powerless. He is powerful in exactly the wrong language.

## Kim Mi So Refuses to Stay Useful

Mi So's strongest beat arrives when she insists on quitting because of misunderstandings tied to her personal life. The episode has already established that public perception can swallow private truth, and now it turns that pressure toward her. She is tired of having her life interpreted through her job.

That distinction matters. If Mi So only wanted less work, Yeong Joon's offer might solve the problem. If she only wanted more respect, promotion could solve part of it. Her contradiction is sharper: she wants reassurance, she wants clarity, and she still wants to leave. Around the later conversation involving **Oh Ji Ran**, Mi So asks again for reassurance about the misunderstanding. That need does not weaken her decision. It explains it.

The episode is careful enough to show that Mi So's resignation is not a clean, icy exit. She is still entangled in the life she is leaving. She still cares about what is assumed, said, and believed. She is leaving dependence, not erasing history.

BollyAI's read: that is why Mi So works immediately as more than the competent secretary archetype. The pilot gives her the visible skill of managing Yeong Joon's world, then gives her the private exhaustion of being mistaken for an extension of it. Her refusal becomes the episode's moral centre. Every time she turns down a solution, she clarifies the real problem.

The pauses before key reveals also help. The dossier notes deliberate silence around early peaks and later turns, and those breaks give the banter needed air. Without them, the pilot would become verbal ping-pong. With them, Mi So's decision sounds less like a bit and more like a boundary.

## The Proposal Turns Romance Into Management

The final movement reframes the resignation around marriage, timing, and dependence. Mi So's desire to date and marry is not a random excuse. It is part of the larger demand to have a life no longer organized around Yeong Joon. She is not asking for a new assignment. She is asking for herself.

Yeong Joon's response is outrageous because it is perfectly in character. At 61 minutes, he proposes: "I, Lee Yeong Joon, will let you marry me." The wording does the damage. He does not confess so much as authorize. Even romance arrives with a stamp of executive approval.

That is a strong end beat for a pilot because it turns the central misunderstanding into a hook. Yeong Joon thinks marriage to him answers the objection. Mi So's objection is that he still cannot imagine a future where her desire is not routed through his permission. The proposal is funny, but it is also a diagnostic test, and he fails it beautifully.

The episode's risk is that Yeong Joon's self-absorption could become too broad. The final line walks close to caricature. The structure saves it. The hour has already shown him treating resignation as HR trouble, promotion as cure, and reassurance as a task to complete. By the time marriage appears, it is the logical next wrong answer.

As a pilot, the episode plants clean open loops: why Mi So is leaving despite the offers, how the personal misunderstanding will surface, and whether a replacement can ever copy what she actually provides.

## The Verdict

"Episode 1" is a sturdy, cleanly premised opener that understands the comic power of a man solving the wrong problem with complete confidence. Its best craft move is making every offer from Yeong Joon sound reasonable until Mi So's refusal exposes the emptiness underneath. The episode weakens when it repeats the resignation misunderstanding without adding a new angle, and the office reaction material can feel broader than the character work around it. But the final proposal earns its absurdity because the hour has built Yeong Joon as a man who mistakes access for intimacy.

BollyAI's score: 7.4/10. As a season opener, it earns its slot by turning a workplace resignation into a romantic power test, while leaving Mi So's deeper reason unresolved enough to pull the story forward.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

verdict.one_liner: A sharp office-romance opener where every grand offer proves Lee Yeong Joon understands power better than Kim Mi So.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 9
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The series pivots into trauma territory here, deepening what had been a light workplace comedy into something with genuine psychological stakes. The tonal shift was the most debated element of the show's run.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The childhood memory revelation - the scene that recontextualises every prior comedic beat and justifies the show's structural gamble.
